title: How a talk gets taken care of

slides.title: How a talk gets taken care of
slides.html:
A talk in three parts

How a talk gets taken care of

An AI agent drafts the deck. A human carries it on stage.
slides.notes: Welcome the room. This talk follows one presentation from a rough brief to the moment it is shared after the stage. Set the frame: an AI agent drafts, a person presents.

slides.title: Agenda
slides.html:
Agenda

Four questions, one talk

  1. Why the pipeline exists
  2. How the agent builds the deck
  3. How the person rehearses and presents
  4. How the talk is shared afterwards
slides.notes: Walk through the four questions quickly. Reveal each item with a click so the room follows the order of the talk.

slides.title: The pipeline at a glance
slides.html:
Overview

The pipeline at a glance

Every stage has one owner. Nothing moves forward without a check.
slides.notes: Point at each box from left to right. Stress that the agent never presents and the person never starts from a blank page.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.html:
Context

Why it matters

  • Preparing a talk can take days of slide work.
  • An agent can draft the structure in minutes.
  • A person keeps the judgment, the voice and the stage.
slides.notes: Name the pain: days of slide work for a talk that lasts twenty minutes. Then state the goal: speed without losing the speaker's voice.

slides.title: From brief to outline
slides.html:
Stage 1

From brief to outline

  1. Write a one-paragraph brief: audience, goal and length.
  2. The agent proposes a storyline with one idea per slide.
  3. The person cuts, reorders and approves the outline.
slides.notes: A good brief is short. Ask for the audience, the goal and the length before anything else. The agent works best when the brief is specific.

slides.title: Structure that holds attention
slides.html:
Stage 1, continued

Structure that holds attention

Open

Start with a question the room already cares about.

Develop

Give three ideas, each with one concrete example.

Close

End with one action the audience can take.
slides.notes: Three ideas is a good default for twenty minutes. Each card reveals on its own step so the structure stays visible.

slides.title: Where the hours go
slides.html:
Effort

Where the hours go

Illustrative numbers for a manual workflow.
slides.notes: These numbers are illustrative, not measured. The point is that drafting and layout take most of the time, which is where the agent helps most.

slides.title: The deck is just JSON
slides.html:
Format

The deck is just JSON

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "title": "My talk",
  "aspectRatio": "16:9",
  "slides": [
    { "id": "cover", "title": "Cover", "html": "<h1>Hello</h1>" }
  ]
}
slides.notes: Show the shape, not the details. Each slide is an object with an id, a title and HTML. The format is strict on purpose so the agent and the player agree.

slides.title: Who owns what
slides.html:
Roles

Who owns what

StageAgentPerson
OutlineProposes the storylineApproves it
SlidesDrafts the HTMLChecks every fact
NotesWrites a first passRewrites them in their own voice
RehearsalEstimates timingPresents
slides.notes: Read the table row by row. The key message is that every stage has one clear owner.

slides.title: What the agent does
slides.html:
Agent

What the agent does

  • Turns the brief into an outline with one idea per slide.
  • Writes slide HTML inside the safe subset of the format.
  • Drafts speaker notes that the person will rewrite.
slides.notes: The agent is fast at structure and first drafts. Be clear that its output is a starting point, not the final talk.

slides.title: What the person does
slides.html:
Person

What the person does

  • Checks every fact and every number on every slide.
  • Rewrites the notes in their own voice.
  • Rehearses, times and presents the talk on stage.
slides.notes: The person owns accuracy, judgment and delivery. Every number and quote needs a human check before the talk.

slides.title: The review loop
slides.html:
Process

The review loop
slides.notes: Explain the loop: draft, review, revise, and repeat. Each pass is short, and the loop ends only when the presenter approves the slide.

slides.title: Run of show
slides.html:
Stage

Run of show
slides.notes: Use the timeline as a plan for the stage. Five marks for twenty minutes keep the pace honest. Adjust the marks to match your own rhythm.

slides.title: Speaker view
slides.html:
Presenter

Speaker view

  • The current slide and the next one appear side by side.
  • The clock shows progress against each section's planned time.
  • Notes stay on the presenter screen and never reach the audience.
slides.notes: Explain what the presenter sees: the current slide, the next one, the notes and the clock. Notes stay private and never reach the audience.

slides.title: Live controls
slides.html:
On stage

Live controls

NextReveal the next step or slide

BackStep back when a point needs repeating

NotesOpen the speaker view for a reminder
slides.notes: Keep the controls simple. Practise next and back until they feel automatic. Use notes only when a detail needs a reminder.

slides.title: Questions from the room
slides.html:
Q and A

Questions from the room

Repeat the question before answering.

Answer in one or two sentences.

Park out-of-scope questions for after the talk.
slides.notes: Repeat each question before answering so the room hears it. Answer briefly and park out-of-scope questions for later.

slides.title: Sharing after the talk
slides.html:
Afterwards

Sharing after the talk

  • Publish a link that hides the speaker notes.
  • Export a PDF for attendees who asked for slides.
  • Keep the JSON file so the next talk starts from this one.
slides.notes: Speaker notes never appear on public links. Share the deck with attendees in a form that matches what they need.

slides.title: Lessons learned
slides.html:
Reflection

Lessons learned

  1. Write the brief before the outline.
  2. Limit each slide to one idea.
  3. Rehearse with the notes the audience never sees.
  4. Keep a person in every review step.
slides.notes: Ask the room which of these lessons matches their experience. Keep the list short and memorable.

slides.title: What can go wrong
slides.html:
Risks

What can go wrong

Invented facts

Check every number and quote before the talk.

Generic voice

Rewrite the notes so they sound like you.

Overflowing text

Keep titles short and check the canvas.
slides.notes: Be honest about the limits. Invented facts, a generic voice and overflowing text are real risks, and each one has a simple check.

slides.title: Thank you
slides.html:
Questions

Thank you

Questions are welcome. The deck and the notes stay in your hands.
slides.notes: Close with thanks and open the floor for questions. Remind the room that the deck and the notes stay in the presenter's hands.
